title: Medicine and Physicians
lead: The Bible's doctors and remedies, and the old question of whether going to a doctor shows a lack of faith. Hebrew uses one word, rophe', "healer," both for human physicians and for the LORD himself (Exodus 15:26). This page is about human medicine; healing by God's direct act, and the anointing of the sick, are under Healing.

sections.b:
Joseph's servants "the physicians" embalm Jacob in Egypt (Genesis 50:2). The law makes a man who injures another pay for the time lost and see "that he is fully healed" (Exodus 21:19). Balm, Hebrew tsori, was carried from Gilead to Egypt as a trade good and a gift (Genesis 37:25; Genesis 43:11), and the prophets use it as a picture of a cure: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no healer there?" (Jeremiah 8:22; compare Jeremiah 46:11; Jeremiah 51:8). Which plant gave it is not known for certain; the Greek translators simply wrote rhētinē, "resin."

Other remedies appear in passing: a lump of pressed figs on King Hezekiah's sore (2 Kings 20:7; Isaiah 38:21); wounds "squeezed clean or bandaged / or eased with oil" (Isaiah 1:6); a broken arm that should have been bound up (Ezekiel 30:21); the Samaritan who "poured oil and wine on his wounds and bandaged them" (Luke 10:34); "a little wine for your stomach" (1 Timothy 5:23); and "eye salve" (Revelation 3:18). In the Book of Tobit, read as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox Christians, Tobias heals his father's blindness with a fish's gall on the angel Raphael's instructions (Tobit 11:11–13).

sections.h: Asa, Job's friends and the doctors of the Gospels
sections.b:
King Asa "fell sick in his feet ... Even in his sickness he did not seek the LORD, only the healers" (2 Chronicles 16:12). The KJV's "physicians" is the same Hebrew word, rophe'im, that names God "your healer" in Exodus 15:26. Job calls his friends "healers of nothing" (Job 13:4). In the Gospels a woman with a flow of blood had suffered under "many doctors" and "only gotten worse" (Mark 5:26); Luke, whom Paul calls "the beloved doctor" (Colossians 4:14), says she had spent all she had on doctors and none could cure her, but does not say she got worse (Luke 8:43). Jesus takes the doctor as a picture of himself: "People who are strong do not need a doctor. Sick people do" (Matthew 9:12), and quotes the proverb "Doctor, cure yourself!" (Luke 4:23).

Was Asa's sin going to doctors at all, or going to them instead of God? Jewish teachers answered differently. The Talmud learns from Exodus 21:19 that "permission is granted to a doctor to heal" (Bava Kamma 85a). Ibn Ezra, on that verse, limited the permission to "blows and wounds that are visible on the surface" and said that illness inside the body is "in God's hand," pointing to Asa. Ramban (on Leviticus 26:11) held that when Israel was fully faithful it would have no need of a physician, and that the Talmud's permission is given to the doctor, who must not refuse a patient who comes to him.

sections.h: Honor the doctor: Sirach and the churches
sections.b:
Sirach 38:1–15, in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, gives the fullest teaching. In the Greek it tells the reader to honor the physician, because the Lord created him; says that the Lord created medicines out of the earth and a sensible person will not despise them, recalling the wood that made the water sweet (Exodus 15:25); tells the sick to pray, turn from sin and bring an offering, and then to give the doctor his place, since doctors too pray to the Lord to give them success. Prayer and medicine stand side by side, as they do in James 5:14, where the elders pray and anoint the sick with oil.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2288) says, "Life and physical health are precious gifts entrusted to us by God. We must take reasonable care of them." Where Christians differ is over divine healing and how far it should be expected now; that debate is under Healing.
